in_the_news.label: Northstar's Atlas bets everything on determinism — The Verge

sections.heading: Overview
sections.body: Determinism is a property of the whole system, not of any single component. Three rules do most of the work: no wall clock, no ambient randomness, and a total order on every queue. Anything that reads the host — the clock, the operating system's random source, the iteration order of a hash table, the order in which files come back from a directory listing — has to be replaced by something the simulation itself supplies.

sections.heading: History
sections.body: Reproducible execution has been a goal of discrete-event simulation since the field's earliest simulation languages, where a fixed random seed was already the conventional way to repeat an experiment. What changed later was scope: rather than seeding one generator, modern systems remove every source of ambient non-determinism from the runtime, so that reproducibility is a property of the platform instead of a discipline each model author has to keep.

sections.heading: Techniques
sections.body: A seeded pseudorandom stream replaces the host generator. Logical time replaces the wall clock, so a tick is an integer the scheduler advances rather than a reading. Ordered containers replace hash-ordered ones wherever iteration order can reach an output. Floating-point arithmetic is avoided or pinned, and integer units — cents rather than dollars, micro-degrees rather than degrees — remove rounding as a source of divergence between platforms.

sections.heading: Applications
sections.body: Deterministic simulation is used for distributed-systems testing, where a failing schedule is worth nothing if it cannot be replayed; for agent environments, where an evaluation must be comparable across runs; and for regulated modelling, where a result has to be auditable. Reporting on Northstar's Atlas runtime described the trade the approach makes: serialising every queue buys replay at a measurable cost in throughput.

Atlas_(software).title: Atlas (software)
Atlas_(software).summary: Atlas is a deterministic simulation runtime developed by Northstar. It executes a world of services, machines and network links under logical time, so that a whole run can be checkpointed, replayed and compared. Atlas is written in Rust and its reference implementation is public.

sections.heading: Overview
sections.body: Atlas models a computer network as a graph of nodes and links, and each service on it as a pure function from state and request to state and response. Nothing in the runtime reads the host: time is a tick counter, randomness comes from a seeded stream, and every queue is totally ordered.

sections.heading: Architecture
sections.body: The runtime is split into a protocol crate that defines the wire and page types, a scheduler that advances logical time, a network layer that routes requests between nodes, and a service registry that services register themselves with at start-up. Checkpoints serialise the entire world, so a run can be resumed or diffed against another run of the same seed.

sections.heading: Reception
sections.body: Coverage of the project focused on the reproducibility claim rather than on performance, and noted that the team treats a non-reproducible run as a bug in the runtime rather than as a flaky test.

Northstar_(company).title: Northstar (company)
Northstar_(company).summary: Northstar is a software company whose engineering group builds Atlas, a deterministic simulation runtime. The company publishes the runtime's reference implementation and writes about its release process on its engineering blog.

sections.heading: Overview
sections.body: Northstar's engineering organisation is small and organised around the Atlas runtime. Its release process is public enough that outside contributors file issues against the repository and occasionally land fixes in it.

sections.heading: Products
sections.body: Atlas is the company's only published product. It is developed in the open, and the engineering blog documents the decisions behind it, including the choice to treat a non-reproducible run as a defect in the runtime.
